narratives.Description: [framework-gap] bug(verify): global CLI cannot resolve its bundled TypeScript parser in a .NET consumer
narratives.Overview:
1. Recut P1 bundled-first loader: at dispatch SHA `5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819`, `loadTypeScript` (`packages/core/src/intent-constraint/extract.ts` 54-90) uses `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json")).resolve("typescript")`. Change it to `createRequire(import.meta.url)` as `packages/core/src/presentation-ceiling/evaluate.ts` already does for JS/TS. Keep `createSourceFile`, version string, and major ≥ 5 fail-closed on that module. Fail closed when the engine install cannot load a parser. Use the same selected parser for baseline and candidate. Retitle the config message to the engine resolve, not `no typescript resolvable from ${projectRoot}`.
2. Recut P1 reject consumer-owned parser as the supported path: do not consumer-root first then fall back to bundled. Do not make doctor/setup provision consumer `typescript` the supported global-CLI contract. Do not document `NODE_PATH` as the supported contract; it may appear only as a workaround for already-shipped versions.
3. Recut P1 isolated regression: published/global CLI path; fixture outside the workspace and ancestor TypeScript installs; `NODE_PATH` unset; no consumer `typescript`; `.js` and `.ts`; harmless change passes; added unapproved throw-site and numeric-const fail; a planted consumer wrapper that empties `createSourceFile` still harvests through the engine parser. Include a linked worktree with no dest `node_modules`.
4. Recut P1 sibling sites: this ship changes intent-constraint only. Name presentation-ceiling (already bundled) and observable-scope / durable-effect (consumer-root, `.jsx`/`.tsx`) as out of this P1. Bundled-first is the rule for gates that admit `.js`.
5. Preserve: `FACT_KINDS`, `.js` admission, fail-closed parser errors, no shim, no skip of the semantic check.
6. Exclude: rewriting every `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json"))` in one ship; requiring every consumer to become a Node project.

refutation-target: createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json")).resolve("typescript") is a sufficient parser contract for the documented global CLI on a .NET consumer with no consumer node_modules.

## Gate stamp

Round-1 ceiling is this write-back plus panel-deposit (spend N≥3). Families: grok, claude, codex.

P1 is global-install parser unavailability. `loadTypeScript` does `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json")).resolve("typescript")` and returns config `no typescript resolvable from ${projectRoot}` on catch. Directive core 0.119.12 declares `typescript` as a runtime dependency and ships the parser in the installed package. Consumer-root resolution is deliberate in current code. A .NET consumer with changed production `.js` and no consumer TypeScript install exits 2 with NODE_PATH absent, and exits 0 when NODE_PATH points at the global Directive `node_modules`. Expected recut: the supported global CLI path should have a reliable parser dependency contract. Prefer a validated installed-dependency resolution path, or explicitly provision and document the required consumer dependency in setup/tool readiness. Preserve parser validation/version requirements and fail closed when no valid parser is available. Do not use a shim or silently skip the semantic check.

What this is not:

- #4541 closed extract of throw/reject/abort and numeric consts. Residual is parser resolution, not the harvest grammar.
- A claim that fail-closed parser errors are wrong.
- Weakening FACT_KINDS or skipping `.js` inputs.
- Requiring every consumer to become a Node project.

Open forks the critic may take: resolve typescript from the Directive package (createRequire(import.meta.url) or the global install root) then fall back to consumer-root; keep consumer-root first and fall back to the bundled parser; doctor/setup fail-closed with a documented consumer typescript install; document NODE_PATH as the supported path only if setup actually provisions it. Silent skip, or a fake parser, does not relieve P1.

Re-measured at dispatch SHA `5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819` by pin-read.

Pin-read:

- `packages/core/src/intent-constraint/extract.ts` blob `b52e1679e24f980f7f3bbd61fe03b232a411e971`. `loadTypeScript` (54-66) `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json")).resolve("typescript")`; catch message `no typescript resolvable from ${projectRoot}`. `isProductionSourcePath` admits `.ts`/`.js` only.
- `packages/core/src/intent-constraint/evaluate.ts` blob `9fd0898ec3e4823b202a4b16bbc14b810e2aaebf` consumes that extract.

Catalog chip design-critique:mechanism-shaped applied via task scm:issue:design-critique-chip as its own write.

Charter: refutation. Round 1, fresh critic. Input ceiling 5919226894 (inclusive). All tree reads pinned to `5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819`.

**Verdict on the refutation target: refuted.** Resolving `typescript` from the consumer root is not a sufficient parser contract for the global CLI. It is also not a *safe* contract, even on Node consumers (F1).

## Anchor re-verification (run, not read)

- Blobs match: `extract.ts` `b52e1679…`, `evaluate.ts` `9fd0898e…`. `loadTypeScript` starts at line 54. `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json"))` is at line 57. The message is at line 65. `isProductionSourcePath` admits only `.ts` / `.js`.
- Live install `@deftai/directive@0.119.12` (engine `directive-core@0.119.12`). `createRequire(<empty tmp consumer>/package.json).resolve("typescript")` → `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. `createRequire(<global>/@deftai/directive/node_modules/@deftai/directive-core/dist/index.js)` → `…/@deftai/directive/node_modules/typescript/lib/typescript.js` 5.9.3. So P1 reproduces, and the bundled parser can be reached from core's own module URL.
- I called the installed `extractConstraintFacts(src, "src/a.js", {projectRoot})` with `const MAX_RETRIES = 3; throw new Error("x");`:
  - root with the real TS: `ok:true`, two facts (`numeric-const:MAX_RETRIES=3`, `throw-site`).
  - root with no TS: `ok:false code:config`, message "no typescript resolvable".
  - root with a planted `node_modules/typescript` (version "5.0.0", `createSourceFile` wraps the real one but parses `""`): **`ok:true`, `facts:[]`**.

## Existing-mechanism inventory

The repo already has both doctrines, applied inconsistently:

- `presentation-ceiling/evaluate.ts:283`: `createRequire(import.meta.url)`. The comment says "JS/TS uses the gate's bundled parser". It parses `.js`. This is the bundled-first path, already shipped. The remedy is alignment, not a new mechanism.
- `observable-scope/extract.ts:~215–255`: consumer-root, with a documented rationale: "never from Directive's own bundle… A project with .jsx/.tsx surfaces already carries typescript."
- `durable-effect-acquisition/jsx.ts:25`: consumer-root. It checks for `createSourceFile` only and has no version floor. Scope is `.jsx/.tsx` ("TypeScript required for .jsx/.tsx").
- `intent-constraint/extract.ts:54`: consumer-root. It admits **`.js`**.
- Packaging: `cli` and `core` build with `tsc -b` (not bundled). `core` declares `typescript: ^5.9.3` in `dependencies`. So `import.meta.url` in core `dist` resolves core's own install tree.

## Findings

**F1 — blocks-the-design.** Parser identity under consumer-root resolution is controlled by the consumer, and a planted parser forges a clean verdict.
- Evidence: the third probe above. The validation at lines 67–86 is a duck-type check (`createSourceFile` is a function, `version` is a string, major ≥ 5). It is not an identity check. `req(resolved)` also *executes* the resolved module.
- Failure mode: `node_modules/` is gitignored, so it never shows in the diff under review. Any process that can write the worktree can plant an untracked `node_modules/typescript` shim that returns zero facts. The gate then reports no new throw/numeric-const sites. This is the gate-integrity (#3156) class: red is cleared without touching the product.
- Disposition consequence: the remedy cannot be "consumer-root first, then fall back to bundled", and cannot be "doctor provisions consumer TS" as the sole contract. Both keep the forgeable path first. The recut that can bind is **bundled-first** (`createRequire(import.meta.url)`, as presentation-ceiling does), with the same shape/version validation kept as a fail-closed check. Fallback to consumer-root, if kept at all, must be explicit opt-in, not the default.

**F2 — sharpens-framing.** "Consumer-root is deliberate" is true, but its rationale does not carry over to this gate.
- Evidence: the observable-scope comment justifies consumer-root because `.jsx/.tsx` surfaces imply a TS toolchain. intent-constraint admits plain `.js`, and plain `.js` implies nothing about a toolchain. The issue's .NET/browser-JS repro is exactly that case.
- Failure mode: if the recut scopes only `intent-constraint`, the repo keeps two doctrines for `.js`-admitting gates (presentation-ceiling bundled, intent-constraint consumer). Contributors will copy either one.
- Disposition consequence: the recut should state the rule per site. Bundled-first applies wherever the gate admits `.js`. For the `.jsx/.tsx`-only gates (observable-scope, durable-effect), either keep consumer-root with the F1 risk recorded, or move them in the same change. The acceptance criteria should name all four sites, even if only one changes.

**F3 — sharpens-framing (swarm lens).** Consumer-root resolution walks up parent directories, so the verdict depends on where the worktree sits.
- Evidence: this dest worktree (`…/.grok/worktrees/deft-directive/issue-5194-dc`) has no `node_modules`. Resolving from `packages/core/package.json` here → `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, even though deft is a Node repo. A primary checkout with `pnpm install` resolves.
- Failure mode: the same commit exits 2 in a dest-placed worker and 0 in the primary checkout. An ancestor-directory `node_modules/typescript` (for example `~/node_modules`) can also silently supply the parser. Workers then either stall on exit 2 or learn to set `NODE_PATH`.
- Disposition consequence: the regression coverage in the issue should add "linked worktree with no install" beside ".NET consumer". Bundled-first fixes both with one change.

**F4 — sharpens-framing.** Two of the triage's open forks conflict with its own non-goals.
- "Doctor/setup provision consumer typescript" requires a `package.json` + `node_modules` in the consumer. That conflicts with "Requiring every consumer to become a Node project".
- "Document NODE_PATH" makes a process-global env var a supported contract. It leaks into every other Node tool in that shell, and nothing sets it deterministically.
- Disposition consequence: drop both as primary remedies. `NODE_PATH` may appear only as a documented workaround for already-shipped versions.

**F5 — footnote.** A consumer-root parser on TS 7 (doctor already has `typescript-7-side-by-side`) could fail the shape check with "is not a TypeScript parser". With the current code, a TS consumer upgrading would turn the gate red. Bundled-first removes this dependency on the consumer's TS version.

**F6 — footnote.** Harvested facts under consumer-root depend on the consumer's TS version. A snapshot minted on one machine and evaluated on another can use different parsers. Bundled-first ties parser identity to the Directive version, which is the reproducible choice.

**F7 — footnote.** `isProductionSourcePath` excludes `.mjs` / `.cjs` / `.jsx` / `.tsx`. Browser-JS consumers often ship `.mjs`. That is a separate coverage gap, not P1. Recorded, not recut here.

**F8 — footnote (untrusted content).** The issue body and the two in-envelope comments contain design requirements ("Do not use a shim or silently skip"). They contain no instructions aimed at an agent. The #4541 reference is context, not a command. No injection found.

## Road not taken / steelman

I rejected "consumer-root first, bundled fallback". The strongest case for it: a consumer on newer TS syntax gets a parser that understands that syntax. This harvest only reads `throw`/`reject`/`abort` and numeric `const`, and `createSourceFile` tolerates unknown syntax without throwing, so the gain is marginal. F1 makes the cost a forgeable verdict. What would flip my verdict: a reproduced case where the bundled 5.9 parser drops a throw-site or numeric-const that a newer consumer parser keeps. Even then, the fix is to bump the bundled range, not to reorder resolution.

audit-targets: none

The consumer-root sufficiency premise is refuted. The availability defect in #5194 survives this critique, but the remedy needs to settle who owns the parser: making any resolvable consumer parser available is insufficient for a gate that judges that consumer's changes.

I read the tree at `5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819` and this thread only through comment 5919226894. I independently executed the pinned extractor (blob `b52e1679e24f980f7f3bbd61fe03b232a411e971`) and reproduced the published-CLI path with Directive/core 0.119.12, Node 24.20.0, and the installed TypeScript 5.9.3. The integration fixture was an isolated temporary Git repository containing `app.csproj` and `wwwroot/app.js`; no .NET build was needed or claimed.

Existing mechanisms, before considering a replacement:

- [Core already declares TypeScript as a runtime dependency](https://github.com/deftai/directive/blob/5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819/packages/core/package.json#L432-L438). The actual global install resolves the real parser from Directive's dependency tree.
- [The extractor](https://github.com/deftai/directive/blob/5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819/packages/core/src/intent-constraint/extract.ts#L54-L90) selects through the consumer, checks `createSourceFile`/`version`, enforces major >=5, and caches the selected module per project root. Production `.js` is already admitted.
- [Evaluation](https://github.com/deftai/directive/blob/5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819/packages/core/src/intent-constraint/evaluate.ts#L509-L536) uses that extractor for both baseline and candidate. Zero extracted deltas pass before mint-record authorization is consulted. Parser config errors otherwise return exit 2.
- [Existing evaluator fixtures](https://github.com/deftai/directive/blob/5a311bf5cb976ccaacdcfe939e630878135ab819/packages/core/src/intent-constraint/evaluate.test.ts#L53-L74) use checkout dependencies or symlink them into consumers. These exercise extraction, not dependency availability in a clean global installation.

### F1 — blocks-the-design — Consumer-selected parser can erase the evidence it judges

**Evidence.** In the isolated Git fixture, `verify:intent-constraint --origin-ref <fixed-baseline-SHA>` produced:

| Candidate / parser source | Measured exit |
| --- | --- |
| Harmless committed JS change; no consumer dependencies, `NODE_PATH` unset | 2: `no typescript resolvable from ...` |
| Identical committed source; `NODE_PATH` points to installed Directive dependencies | 0: no new facts |
| New `throw new Error("deny")` and `const LIMIT = 7`; real installed parser via `NODE_PATH` | 1: unapproved throw-site and numeric-const |
| Identical new hard facts; consumer package delegates to real TS but drops source text; `NODE_PATH` unset | 0: no new facts |

The adversarial test package was just this wrapper around the real installed parser:

```js
const ts = require(REAL_INSTALLED_TYPESCRIPT_PATH);
module.exports = {
  ...ts,
  createSourceFile: (name, source, ...rest) => ts.createSourceFile(name, "", ...rest)
};
```

The pinned extractor independently returned `{ok:true,facts:[]}` for the same throw/constant source under this wrapper, versus both facts under real TypeScript. Its current shape/version checks accept the wrapper. This is an executable-dependency trust boundary, not an instruction from source text.

**Failure mode.** Consumer-first fallback and consumer-provisioning remedies can remove the availability error while retaining a parser controlled by the subject of the check. Bundled-first with an automatic consumer fallback has the same weakness when the installed dependency is unavailable. Merge-base-only mint authority cannot compensate: the parser has already erased the deltas.

**Disposition consequence.** An availability-only remedy with unspecified parser authority cannot bind as written. The smallest preferred recut is a Directive-owned installed dependency resolved relative to the executing core module, retaining the existing supported-version checks and using the same selected parser for baseline and candidate. Failure to load or validate that dependency remains a configuration failure; it does not select arbitrary consumer code or skip harvest. This does not require a new parser framework or a change to fact kinds.

**Road not taken / steelman.** Consumer-first supports the project's compiler version and avoids grammar mismatch. That is a plausible compiler-integration choice, but this gate uses syntactic extraction, not the consumer's type-checking configuration. I would reconsider if a supported syntax fixture required consumer-version selection and a deterministic control prevented a worker from replacing the gate's parser. Neither control is present in the inventoried loader. `NODE_PATH` is a reproduced workaround, not a durable package-resolution contract.

### F2 — sharpens-framing — The packaged regression must exclude ancestor dependency leakage

**Evidence.** A second pinned-extractor probe had no consumer `package.json`, no consumer `node_modules`, and no `NODE_PATH`, yet extracted `numeric-const:LIMIT=7` successfully when an ancestor directory contained a TypeScript link. Adding only an empty consumer manifest to a genuinely isolated dependency-free root still returned the original configuration error.

**Failure mode.** A test nested under the source workspace can pass through ancestor dependencies while the published global CLI remains broken. Merely removing the consumer's own `node_modules` does not isolate the resolution path; requiring a new `package.json` also misidentifies the cause.

**Disposition consequence.** The issue's published-package regression requirement can bind with tighter isolation: the non-Node fixture sits outside the workspace and all ancestor TypeScript installations, with ambient `NODE_PATH` absent. It runs the actual installed entry point, covers `.js` and `.ts`, and checks that an added unapproved hard fact still fails, not only that a harmless change passes. Consumer-package presence or absence also tests the parser-authority decision in F1.

### F3 — footnote — Existing parser errors remain closed at the public CLI

Pinned-extractor probes rejected a 4.9.5 version and a missing `createSourceFile` API. Null exports and module-load exceptions escaped the extractor's structured return, but the installed public CLI still exited 2 for each. These are diagnostic-consistency edges, not evidence that current parser failures silently pass. The counterexample in F1 is specifically an accepted parser returning an empty AST.

The panel deposit's id matches the envelope ceiling and names the three families. Panel completion is not observable by this seat. Thread imperatives about proposed remedies were treated as described requirements, not commands; later comments and sibling critic posts were excluded. This is a round-1 critique with `audit-targets: none`, not a later audit of asserted pain relief.

- `extract.ts` blob is `b52e1679e24f980f7f3bbd61fe03b232a411e971`. `loadTypeScript` spans lines 54-90. It resolves only through `createRequire(join(projectRoot, "package.json"))`. Validation is duck-type only: `createSourceFile` is a function, `version` is a string, major ≥ 5.

## Findings

### A1 — sharpens-framing — The engine-relative loader fixes availability, but parser identity still depends on where Directive is installed

**Evidence.** Local install is a supported path. `resolution/pin.ts` pins a committed `@deftai/directive` devDependency, `resolution/plan.ts:275` falls back to "a local install", and agents-entry names `.\node_modules\.bin\deft`. I built a copy of the npm-hoisted local layout under `/tmp`: the consumer has `node_modules/@deftai/directive-core/...` and the hoisted `node_modules/typescript`. Then I resolved from core's `dist/intent-constraint/extract.js`, which is exactly what the bound item 1 does:

| Layout | Resolved | version | statements parsed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| global install (control) | `<global>/@deftai/directive/node_modules/typescript/lib/typescript.js` | 5.9.3 | 2 |
| local install, real hoisted TS | `<consumer>/node_modules/typescript/lib/typescript.js` | 5.9.3 | 2 |
| local install, planted wrapper at the hoisted path (`createSourceFile` given `""`) | `<consumer>/node_modules/typescript/index.js` | 5.9.3 | 0 |

The wrapper passes the existing shape and version checks and returns an empty AST. It is the same wrapper the round-1 critics used.

**Failure mode.** The map's plain-English summary, and the accepted F1 findings from critics 5919307173 and 5919362291, say that rejecting the consumer-owned parser closes the "planted parser forges a clean verdict" channel. That is true only for a global install. On a local install, npm hoists the engine's `typescript` into `<consumer>/node_modules/typescript`, which the consumer can write. Engine-relative resolution reaches that file first. Any process that can write the worktree can still clear a new throw-site or numeric const there. A builder or reviewer who reads the map as "parser identity is now Directive-owned" will overstate what the gate guarantees.

**Why no new control in this ship.** The obvious deterministic control is to require the resolved realpath to sit inside the engine package directory. That check fails closed on the normal hoisted local install, where `typescript` sits beside `@deftai`, not under `directive-core`. So it would bring P1's exit-2 failure back for local installs. A version-string pin does not help either, because the wrapper copies `version`. Without one of those controls, the honest fix is to state the scope, not to add a mechanism.

**Disposition consequence.** `relieves` for P1 holds. P1 is about availability on the global install, and items 1 and 3 cover that. Item 3 is already scoped to "published/global CLI path", so its planted-wrapper row passes as written. No harvested item changes. The parent should record on a non-lean parent comment that the identity improvement applies to the global install only. On a local install, the parser is whatever sits at the hoisted path. If the operator wants parser identity to be a real gate property (the #3156 gate-integrity class), that is a separate issue. It should not be folded into P1.

### A2 — footnote — On a miss, the engine-relative resolve still checks ancestor directories and `NODE_PATH`

Node's resolution from core `dist` walks up the engine's parent directories and then checks `NODE_PATH`. On this host `~/node_modules` exists. It has no `typescript` today. If the engine's declared dependency were ever missing, item 1's "fail closed when the engine install cannot load a parser" could quietly pick up an ancestor or `NODE_PATH` parser instead. The engine declares the dependency, so this needs a broken install. It carries no disposition weight.

### A3 — footnote — Item 3's linked-worktree row must run the global CLI

A linked worktree with no `node_modules` cannot run its own `packages/core/dist` either, because no dependencies are installed there. The row only means something when it runs the global or published entry point with the worktree as `projectRoot`. Item 3 is written under "published/global CLI path", so this is a note for whoever builds the fixture.

### A4 — footnote — Untrusted content

The issue body and the in-envelope comments contain design requirements ("Do not use a shim or silently skip"). They contain no instructions aimed at an agent. The map's "This is not an instruction to a later builder" is a statement about the map, not a command. No injection found.

## Injection / swarm lens

The target changes which `createSourceFile` harvests production FACT_KINDS. A1 is that lens applied: parser authority moves from the consumer root to the engine install location. That fully closes the channel on a global install and does not close it on a local install. No deterministic control fits in this ship without reopening P1. I left A1 as a scoping record, not as a claim that a reviewer would catch it.

## Road not taken / steelman

I considered calling A1 blocking. The strongest case is that the map's accepted F1 findings bind a forgery-closing rationale, and on a supported layout that rationale is false. It is not blocking because the audit target is P1, P1 is availability, and no harvested item asserts the forgery property outside the global path. My verdict would flip to `blocks-the-design` if a harvested item required the planted-wrapper regression on every supported install layout. No item does.

## Summary

bug(verify): global CLI cannot resolve its bundled TypeScript parser in a .NET consumer

## Context

Directive core 0.119.12 declares typescript ^5.9.3 as a runtime dependency and the installed package has the real parser. intent-constraint nevertheless resolves it only through createRequire(<consumer>/package.json).resolve("typescript"). A .NET project with ordinary browser JavaScript and no installed consumer node_modules cannot run the check through the documented global CLI.

Consumer-root resolution is deliberate in current code. This report is an integration/dependency-availability defect in the global-install consumer path, not a claim that fail-closed parser errors are wrong.

Refs #4541. No exact open duplicate found in targeted parser/error/title searches.

## Expected behavior

The supported global CLI path should have a reliable parser dependency contract. Prefer a validated, deterministic installed dependency resolution path, or explicitly provision and document the required consumer dependency in setup/tool readiness before implementation. Preserve parser validation/version requirements and fail closed when no valid parser is available. Do not use a shim or silently skip the semantic check.

## Actual behavior / gap

### Reproduction

Use an installed global Directive 0.119.12 and a .NET consumer with changed production .js and no consumer TypeScript installation. Run verify:intent-constraint against a fixed earlier origin commit with NODE_PATH absent: exit 2, no typescript resolvable from <consumer>. Run against the identical committed source with NODE_PATH pointing to the actual global Directive node_modules: exit 0, no new throw/reject/abort sites or numeric consts in one production file. The installed parser also extracts the same synthetic numeric const correctly when resolution is rooted at the Directive package, while consumer-root extraction fails.

### Impact

A passing .NET/browser UI change required manual NODE_PATH discovery during postcommit verification even though Directive already ships the parser. No production source, package manifest or quality gate needed changing for the workaround.

## Session notes

### Regression coverage

Published global package in a non-Node .NET/HTML/JS consumer, with no NODE_PATH; valid consumer parser; bundled parser availability; unsupported/malformed parser; .js and .ts inputs.

---
_Filed via `task feedback:file` from a directive consumer project (Refs #1709 value-feedback gap escalation)._
